title: Not scattered, not stuck
hook: attention not scattered outward, not stuck inward
carry: neither flies off nor holds on

segments.voice: Yesterday: joy from having and joy from letting go, and your line, climb through it. Did you find the second one? Today closes a week, and Mahakaccana is back. Day five hundred four.

There are two ways to lose an afternoon. One: forty tabs open, three conversations, half-watching a video, attention flying outward in every direction. Two: stuck in your own head, replaying a comment from last week, or so absorbed in a pleasant daydream you forget to eat. One scatters, one sticks. The hundred and thirty-eighth discourse names both. The Buddha gives a short instruction and goes into his dwelling. The monks, just as with the bhaddekaratta verse, go looking for Mahakaccana. Today: not scattered.
screen: `FORTY TABS OPEN.` → `STUCK IN YOUR OWN HEAD.` → `THE MONKS GO TO MAHAKACCANA.`

segments.voice: Here's the Buddha's instruction, in paraphrase. A monk should examine things in such a way that his consciousness isn't scattered and spread out externally, isn't stuck internally, and, not clinging, isn't agitated. Then there's no more birth, aging and death. That's all. He goes in. Mahakaccana unpacks it. Scattered outward, he says, is when the eye sees a form and consciousness follows the attractive look of it, tied to its pleasure, chained to it. Same for sounds, smells, tastes, touches and ideas. That's the forty tabs. Stuck inward is subtler. It's when someone reaches a calm, joyful meditative state and then gets attached to the joy of it, bound by its pleasure. Even good stillness can become a place to hide. And agitation from clinging? That's taking the body, feelings, perceptions, formations or consciousness as myself, and then being shaken when they change. Mahakaccana's explanation puts the middle in an unusual place. Not halfway between busy and calm, but beyond both habits: attention that can go out to the world without being dragged away, and come home without being glued there. The Buddha, hearing it, approves. Look back at the week: five messengers at Yama's court, one fine night, the verse explained, heirs of our deeds, more complex than it looks, two joys. And now a mind that neither flies off nor holds on.
screen: `A BRIEF SAYING, THEN SILENCE` · `SCATTERED: CHASING WHAT'S SEEN` · `STUCK: CLINGING TO CALM` · `AGITATED: TAKING IT AS ME` · then, large: `NOT SCATTERED, NOT STUCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep attention home. Sit and settle on the breath. When attention flies out, to a sound, a plan, a screen, notice: scattered. Gently come back. When you find yourself sinking into a pleasant fog, or circling one thought, notice: stuck. Gently open up again, to the whole body, the room. Home isn't a cell. It's a doorway you can stand in. The bell holds the time.
Not scattered. Attention that isn't dragged outward by what it sees, and isn't stuck inward in its own calm. Today's word.
Your line: neither flies off nor holds on. Today, close one tab you don't need, and step out of one thought you've been circling. Day five hundred four.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools warn both against distraction and against becoming attached to pleasant meditative states, and students are taught to notice each without forcing.

myth: in MN 138 being stuck inward can mean clinging to the joy of meditation
Mahakaccana says even a calm, joyful state can become something to cling to.
the Buddha explains the saying in full detail himself
he gives it briefly and goes inside; Mahakaccana explains it, and the Buddha approves.
the discourse says attention should never go outward
the trouble is being dragged away by attraction, not seeing the world at all.

fork.setup: you've reached a calm, joyful state in meditation, and you never want to leave it. in Mahakaccana's terms, what's happening?
options: consciousness is stuck inward, bound by the joy of it.
fork.reveal: being bound to the pleasure of a meditative state is what Mahakaccana calls being stuck internally.

original.note: Pali vikkhitta: scattered, distracted. the Buddha's saying: not scattered externally, not stuck internally.

trapdoor: what you thought: the problem is distraction, so the answer is to go inward.
what it means: you can be scattered outward or stuck inward, and both are traps.
what a scholar hears: MN 138, the Uddesavibhanga Sutta, follows the same uddesa-and-vibhanga pattern as MN 133, with Mahakaccana again expanding the Buddha's brief saying.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 138, Uddesavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of a summary)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'You know'.

MN 138 paraphrased. Confirm Mahakaccana's explanation: externally scattered as following the sign (nimitta) of forms with gratification; internally stuck as attached to the rapture or pleasure of the jhanas; agitation through clinging as identity view.
Confirm the Pali 'bahiddha avikkhittam avisatam, ajjhattam asanthitam' phrasing behind 'not scattered, not stuck'.
